claim: In a 2017 survey of 382 YouTubers and streamers, 208 respondents (53.9%) reported earning no income at all from content creation; only 174 (46.1%) reported any income.
stance_target: A majority of people who identify as content creators earn literally nothing, so any 'average creator income' computed over earners only is a selection artefact.
scope_conditions: N=382 self-selected respondents recruited via Facebook groups, subreddits and direct messaging on YouTube/Twitch/Vidme, fielded 2017. Sample is Finland 39%, US 31.9%, Other 29.1%. Because recruitment reached only currently-ACTIVE creators, the true zero-income share across everyone who ever started is higher.
region: Finland 39% (n=149), US 31.9% (n=122), Other 29.1% (n=111). NO Southeast Asian representation reported — US/Nordic-dominated, does not generalize to SEA.

claim: The most work-oriented content creators in the sample spent 25.00 hours per week producing content plus 11.88 hours per week on promotional social media, yet earned a mean total income of only $774.85 (SD $1,999.79, n=48).
stance_target: Even the highest-effort, most professionally-oriented creators in a general creator population earn amounts far below a living wage relative to the hours invested.
scope_conditions: n=48 of 382; 'work-oriented' defined as a mean score below 3.75 on a 7-point work-play perception scale. Income was self-reported as an estimate chosen from a list of frequency bands, with the maximum value of the band used — biasing the reported figure UPWARD. The paper does not state the income period (total/annual/lifetime).
quoted_support: It seems that individuals who perceive the activity more as work, are the ones who spend the most hours per week on video content creation itself (M = 25.00 h), as well as the most average time on personal broadcasting related social media activities (M = 11.88 h). Additionally, they appear to be earning the most income on average out of the examined groups (M = $774.85)

claim: Tenure in content creation did not significantly predict income: the group with the longest mean tenure (38.67 months) earned $179.11 while the group with the shortest (34.21 months) earned $774.85, and the ANOVA on tenure was non-significant (F=0.801, p=0.405).
stance_target: The assumption that persisting in content creation for longer reliably converts into higher income — i.e. that 'time to first meaningful income' is mainly a function of elapsed time rather than of intensity and strategy.
scope_conditions: Cross-sectional, N=382, 2017. Tenure measured in months active. Groups are perception-based (work / playbour / play), not tenure-matched, so this is a correlational not causal refutation. Survivorship bias cuts the other way here: creators who quit early are absent, which if anything should strengthen a positive tenure-income relationship, and it still does not appear.
quoted_support: The findings related to the tenure (p = 0.405) variable were found insignificant based on the results of the one-way ANOVA seen in Table 4. ... Despite being the most active in their broadcasting and the highest earners of the three groups, individuals who perceive personal broadcasting as work are not the ones with the most experience from these activities (M = 34.21 months).

claim: Reported creator income standard deviations exceeded group means by factors of 2.6x to 4.6x, quantifying an extreme right-skew in which a handful of respondents account for nearly all income.
stance_target: Mean creator earnings are not a meaningful central-tendency statistic; medians and full distributions are required.
scope_conditions: N=382, 2017. Work group mean $774.85 / SD $1,999.79 (2.58x); playbour mean $145.76 / SD $587.66 (4.03x); play mean $179.11 / SD $818.15 (4.57x). The paper does not report medians, which is itself a reporting gap for this research question.
quoted_support: Total income ($) Work Mean ... 774.85 ... Std. Deviation ... 1999.79 ... Eq. Work and Play Mean ... 145.76 ... Std. Deviation ... 587.66 ... Play Mean ... 179.11 ... Std. Deviation ... 818.15

claim: The largest single group of creators in the sample (268 of 382, 70.2%) treated content creation as play rather than work, investing 13.28 hours per week and earning a mean of $179.11.
stance_target: Most people in creator populations are hobbyists, not occupational workers, which means population-level attrition statistics conflate hobby lapse with occupational failure.
scope_conditions: N=382, 2017; perception-based grouping with cut-off >4.25 on the 7-point scale for the play group.
quoted_support: The final group examined in this research and incidentally, the largest group identified in our sample, is the group of content creators who identified the activity as more play than work. This play-oriented group has the longest experience from the activity (M = 38.67 months).

claim: The 25 hours per week of production time measured for work-oriented creators explicitly excludes promotional, administrative and organisational tasks, so the true occupational time burden is materially larger than the headline figure.
stance_target: Published creator hours figures systematically undercount total occupational labour.
scope_conditions: Author caveat in the discussion section of the HICSS-52 paper; applies to the n=48 work-oriented subgroup.
quoted_support: It should be noted that even for those personal broadcasters, who create video content as their full-time employment, this level of activity would constitute nearly half of the weekly average working hours, which also excludes all promotional and administrative or organisational tasks, that are also associated with this type of independent work.
numbers: 'nearly half' of a standard working week

claim: Two-thirds of surveyed creators were simultaneously in full-time work or full-time study (33.7% employed full-time, 35.5% students), with a further 16.3% unemployed and only 13.2% part-time.
stance_target: Content creation functions predominantly as a supplemental or secondary activity rather than a primary occupation, even among creators active enough to be recruited into research.
scope_conditions: N=382, 2017; self-reported employment status. Age skew: 43.0% aged 18-24, 33.2% aged 24-34, 8.8% under 17. Gender: 73.6% male, 25.1% female.
quoted_support: Employment Part-time 51 13.2% ... Full-time 128 33.7% ... Student 135 35.5% ... Unemployed 63 16.3% ... Retired 5 1.3%

claim: The sample was recruited entirely from currently-active creators via platform-affiliated channels, so it structurally cannot observe anyone who already quit — a survivorship bias the authors do not quantify.
stance_target: That cross-sectional creator surveys can measure attrition rates or the earnings of the full population of people who attempt content creation.
scope_conditions: Applies to this study and, by extension, to the entire class of self-selected creator surveys. The authors acknowledge only the generic limitation that a survey 'provides a specific vantage point on an individual's perceptions and views of reality', not the sampling-frame problem.
quoted_support: The survey was distributed through various digital channels such as Facebook groups and subreddits related to specific video content genres and distribution services. Various personal broadcasters were also approached through email and messaging services of platforms such as YouTube, Twitch and Vidme (closed in 2017).
